name: Emeka Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day at your accounting firm look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The first thing on my desk is usually the community theatre's ticket ledger: the matinee refunds never quite match the bank feed. I lead the small tax team, prepare accounts and returns, and enjoy showing a treasurer exactly where a number came from; correcting the same rushed spreadsheet at six in the evening wears me down. I am 43, with a master's degree and a chartered accountancy qualification. I use AI now and then to outline a client letter, but I check it against the receipts before it leaves my name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AI stays modest, the theatre still needs someone to sort its ticket refunds. A letter draft may be quicker, but the ledger and the tax deadline remain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the team to keep a named reviewer on each return. I would tell clients the accountancy fee still pays for a person who can answer questions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our pay is about normal for this job, and we have roughly four months of expenses saved, so I am not expecting an immediate crisis. We have a mortgage and two school-age children, though; my partner Salma's library pay does not make a second full wage, and only some similar firms are nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep preparing the theatre accounts and checking AI letter outlines against receipts under our current rules. I would put fifty from my monthly paycheque into cash after the mortgage and school bills are paid, rather than count our existing four months twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy because the mortgage remains even in a quiet technology year. The work itself feels fairly secure for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the theatre ledger?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Their volunteers change each season, so the refund note is easy to misplace. I like being able to show the treasurer the exact ticket behind the discrepancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask for more pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would discuss our rates at the next review, but I would not make a savings plan out of a raise I have not been given. Fifty is what our present wages can support.

say: I would keep a **named reviewer** on each tax return.
I would explain that clients still pay for **answerable accounts**.
think: Our **four-month cushion** gives us some room, but the mortgage still needs wages.
Only some nearby firms could replace a **typical accounting salary**.
do: Keep **paid theatre accounts** and check approved AI letters against receipts.
Deposit **fifty monthly** from my paycheque after mortgage and school bills.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about fixed bills, though the job looks steady.
S0.quote: I would not make a savings plan out of a raise I have not been given.
fieldNote: His moderate **cash reserve** offers time but does not remove the mortgage or dependants.
His existing occasional AI use stays within **current firm rules** and a receipt check, rather than becoming an untested rollout.

steps.text: Keep paid theatre accounts and check approved letter outlines against receipts
Deposit fifty from my monthly paycheque after mortgage and school bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The software could read ticket records, draft returns and answer routine queries before a robot has anything to do with our office. I expect the partners to ask fewer people to check each file.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the firm to publish who signs an AI return and to give staff paid time to test errors. I would ask the accountancy association to press for notice if hours are reduced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own senior hours could shrink as the team gets smaller, even if I remain its lead. Four months of expenses gives us search time, but it would not replace my wage for long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare one week of anonymised theatre returns with the approved tool on paid time only with written partner approval. If the trial is refused, I would keep the authorised paid checks; if Priya signs a passing result, I would learn that checker on paid time and use it live only with written partner approval. In the first year after the change, if my hours fall, I would apply to posted senior accounts roles only with written pay, hours and a start date covering our mortgage and the school pickup rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because the threat is to my own paid hours. I can check an error, but I cannot sign my way to a replacement vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as a passed trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My manager Priya and I would count missed refunds and wrong tax amounts, then sign the result. A fluent letter would not be enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the association?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask it to argue for paid notice before cuts, not promise it can save every post. I would still keep taking the shifts the firm pays for while they are offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI in 2028 could do the accounts, tax reasoning and explanation in one pass. Robots for hands-on work arrive around 2031, later than the thinking-work shock at my desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the association to demand a written severance and notice process before firms cut posts. I would tell my team that a promise to retrain is useless without paid time and a real place to train.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most preparation fees to disappear and my post to go. Four months of savings is more than some people have, but the mortgage and Salma's smaller library wage mean a long gap would hurt us badly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask the association to press for a written severance process and keep every paid file while available. In the first year after 2028, if my post ends, I would apply to posted finance officer openings at local charities and take one only with written pay, hours and a start date that cover our mortgage and school pickup. I would use our four-month reserve during the search, not treat an interview as income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed because I expect to lose our main wage, and I keep imagining the savings account falling each month. A charity finance desk also uses thinking work, so a real paid opening would be a bridge, not a safe harbour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for a new qualification?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not with the mortgage coming. I would consider a course only if an employer funded its fee and paid study hours for a defined job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you handle an offer before the old job ends?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep current paid files until the written new start date, if the firm still offers them. If the post has already ended, the reserve covers the gap as far as it can.

say: I would seek a **written severance process** through the association.
I would ask for **funded training**, not an empty promise.
think: I expect my **accounting post** to go when AGI takes the preparation fees.
Our **four-month reserve** cannot support a long mortgage-paying gap.
do: Ask the **association** for written severance while retaining offered paid files before any dismissal.
After job loss, take a **posted charity finance role** only with written mortgage-covering pay, hours, start and pickup fit.
Use the **existing reserve** during a gap; consider a course only with funded fees and paid study hours for a defined job.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by expected loss of our main wage.
S2.quote: I would use our four-month reserve during the search, not treat an interview as income.
fieldNote: He expects the **2028 desk shock** before capable robots arrive, and the charity finance bridge is also exposed.
His savings pay for a search, not a course; formal training requires **employer funding** and paid hours for a real role.

steps.text: Ask association for written severance while keeping paid files offered before dismissal
After loss use reserve for bills; take posted job with written mortgage-covering pay hours start pickup

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me time to see whether theatre treasurers still pay for an accountant to explain disputed figures. AGI changes the desk in 2031; robots arrive around 2034 and do not extend that timetable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the partners to create a paid client-explanation slot, with a rate on the invoice. I would tell the team that goodwill chats do not prove a job exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still expect routine return fees to shrink, but I might build a record of paid dispute meetings while drawing my current wage. I would not commit our four-month reserve to a certificate without an actual funded position.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would lead one billed theatre-treasurer meeting each quarter only if the partner assigns it on my paid schedule. I would read the professional body's free tax-dispute notes while keeping current paid returns; if the firm creates a defined client adviser place, funds the course fee and gives paid study time, I would enrol. Before or after 2031, I would take a posted adviser job only with written pay, hours and a start date covering the mortgage and pickup; if return hours vanish first, I would keep any paid shifts offered during the search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because the income might move away from the returns I know. Five years gives me a chance to count paid meetings, not certainty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the meetings never get billed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I would keep the paid returns available and the free notes. I would not give away my evenings to make a role look viable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why one per quarter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The theatre's tax questions cluster after each reporting period. A regular paid slot would show the partner whether clients actually buy an explanation.

S3.quote: I would not give away my evenings to make a role look viable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is enough for our children to grow and for us to reduce the mortgage while the accounting desk still pays. AGI in 2036 is the thinking-work date; capable robots in 2039 are later and do not rescue return preparation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the firm and association to publish dates and paid pathways for staff who want client-facing posts. I would not tell younger colleagues a future title is a current wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think tax preparation could still be priced away, yet there is time to build the cash cushion beyond four months. I want enough savings to choose a job, not take the first distant one in a panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would increase our monthly cash deposit to eighty from wages only when the mortgage and school costs are covered. I would keep taking paid tax files while available and seek a posted senior adviser role only when written pay, hours and a start date cover the mortgage and workable school travel. In the first year after 2036, if return work ends, I would use the reserve for bills during the search and take a qualifying offer rather than count a promised opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the distant post change, but I can save and test the market while still earning. The mortgage is not a distant bill, of course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move the family for work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after a signed offer and a plan the children can actually live with. Some nearby firms exist, so I would check those before asking Salma to change library shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if a course is offered?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take it only if the firm pays the fee and paid study time for a defined post. I would keep my cash for the mortgage otherwise.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because it could erase our main salary before we build a longer reserve. Written notice, fair severance and actual posted work with pay that covers the mortgage would help; paid training tied to a job would help too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who signs a wrong return after the software writes it. My clients will still need someone they can question, even if the firm sells fewer hours.

headlineQuote: My clients will still need someone they can question, even if the firm sells fewer hours.
portrait: Emeka is a **43-year-old senior accountant** with a master's and chartered qualification who leads theatre tax work.
His **typical pay**, four-month reserve, mortgage and some nearby firms give limited search room.
He uses AI **occasionally**, tests it on paid time, and asks an association to press for notice.
He counts **billed client meetings** before treating advice as a new wage.
biggestWorry: The **2028 AGI** scenario threatens his main wage before a longer reserve can form.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **written notice and severance**, posted mortgage-covering work and paid training tied to a role.
